guides.title: Use nanites for time and silos for a specific threat.
guides.summary: Decide when a Nanite Factory is worth the investment, reserve mixed missile capacity and understand what an IPM attack actually changes.
guides.label: Planet infrastructure
guides.status: Checked 8 November 2026. Construction examples are unmodified baselines; an archived missile flight-time discrepancy is explicitly flagged. Confirm displayed costs and timers in your universe.
objectives: Distinguish construction throughput from resource production.
Compare a Nanite upgrade with the queues it will accelerate.
Calculate a legal mix of Anti-Ballistic and Interplanetary Missiles.
Check range, interception and irreversible launch consequences before firing.

sections.title: Unlock the capability you actually need
paragraphs: Nanite Factories and Missile Silos are planet facilities. Build them where their effect is needed; a Nanite on one planet does not accelerate another planet or its moon. The following are standard base costs before applicable modifiers. Facility costs double with each successive level.

callout.title: Capacity does not come preloaded
callout.text: An empty Silo provides no interception. After unlocking ABMs, you must actually build them in the defense production menu.

sections.title: What a Nanite Factory accelerates
paragraphs: Each completed Nanite level halves the standard construction time of buildings, ships and defense at that planet. Relative to Nanite 0, levels 1, 2, 3 and 4 give factors of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16. It does not directly increase mine output or speed ordinary research.

Robotics affects building construction; Shipyard affects ships and defense. Keep these roles distinct when diagnosing a slow queue. A higher Robotics level is not a substitute for Shipyard levels when producing a fleet.

Schedule a Nanite upgrade around local production. An active ship/defense queue can block the upgrade from starting, and Nanite construction blocks those production jobs. Adding an order to a queue is not the same as its being able to start. Finish needed ABMs or emergency ships before taking that production capacity offline.

sections.title: Read a baseline construction calculation
paragraphs: For an ordinary building upgrade beyond the early-level speed-up, the baseline time in hours is (Metal + Crystal cost) ÷ [2,500 × (Robotics level + 1) × 2ᴺ × economy speed], where N is the already completed Nanite level. For ships and defense, use Shipyard level in place of Robotics. Deuterium cost is not part of this timing numerator.

The example assumes no Lifeform reductions, other modifiers or acceleration items. The game applies whole-second timing and minimum durations, so doubling a very fast facility is not necessarily useful for a unit already at the minimum. Use the displayed timer for the actual purchase.

callout.title: Do not apply this blindly to Lifeforms
callout.text: Lifeform buildings have their own scaling and modifiers. This table explains the classic construction factor; it is not a complete formula for every Lifeform building or technology.

sections.title: Buy time when time is the bottleneck
steps: List the next three construction or production jobs on the planet, their displayed durations and whether you can fund them.
Estimate how much of that schedule the next Nanite level saves. Include the Nanite’s own cost and the period during which its construction occupies or blocks local work.
Compare against the other bottleneck: if you wait days for resources and the queue is empty, faster production may not help immediately. If funded jobs are backed up, throughput has clear value.
Keep fuel, cargo replacement and essential defense reserves separate from the upgrade budget. Do not turn a convenience purchase into an unsafe transport situation.
When the upgrade completes, confirm its level and inspect the next job’s duration before filling a long queue. Record the result so that the next comparison uses your account’s actual modifiers.

example.title: A simple time comparison, not a resource-payback claim
example.text: Suppose the next funded work takes 48 hours at the current level. Halving it saves approximately 24 hours, but a Nanite upgrade occupying 30 hours would not make that short sequence finish earlier. A much longer funded backlog changes the answer. Earlier mine completion may also earn resources, which requires a separate production calculation.

sections.title: Reserve capacity for both missile types
paragraphs: A Silo provides 10 capacity units per level. One ABM uses one unit and one IPM uses two: ABM count + 2 × IPM count must not exceed 10 × Silo level. Upgrading the Silo increases capacity, not missile range.

Choose a defensive reserve before filling the rest with offensive missiles. Once ABMs intercept an attack they are consumed, so remaining stock matters more than the Silo’s level. The planet’s ABMs also protect its moon against IPMs; you cannot build a separate Silo on the moon.

rows: More offense means less interception reserve

callout.title: Do not demolish first and ask later
callout.text: The archived official guide requires an empty Silo before demolition. Removing stored missiles is a separate destructive decision; upgrading the Silo is possible without emptying it. Inspect the current control and consequences before clearing anything.

sections.title: Know what missiles destroy and what stops them
paragraphs: An ABM automatically destroys one incoming IPM and is itself consumed. Surviving IPMs attack defense, not the fleet or buildings. They ignore shields, and destroyed defenses do not receive the normal post-combat rebuilding chance. Attacker Weapons Technology and defender Armour Technology matter to the result.

Choose a primary defense type when launching. The aim is to remove a particular obstacle, not assume that one missile always destroys one turret. Use a current missile-capable simulator with the target’s technologies and defenses. Re-scout after impact before sending a fleet.

example.title: Interception comes before damage
example.text: If a planet has 12 ABMs and receives 20 IPMs, 12 missiles are intercepted and at most 8 reach the defenses, assuming no ABMs are added or consumed by another strike in the meantime. Those eight still need a damage calculation; “eight missiles” does not mean “eight Plasma Turrets destroyed”.

sections.title: Separate missile range from travel time
paragraphs: The standard range is 5 × Impulse Drive level − 1 systems, within the same galaxy. Impulse 6 reaches 29 systems either way. Where circular solar systems are enabled, measure across the shorter wraparound route. Circular galaxies do not let an IPM cross into another galaxy.

The archived Formula Thread gives the baseline flight time as 30 + 60 × system distance seconds, divided by the relevant fleet-speed factor. The Origin universe-settings guide classifies missile attacks as war missions. Thus, ten systems at ×2 war speed give a baseline 315 seconds, or 5 minutes 15 seconds.

callout.title: An archive inconsistency matters here
callout.text: The archived IPM Guide instead prints 30 + 30 × distance. Because the official archives disagree, this lesson uses the Formula Thread baseline for explanation, not a guaranteed live countdown. Verify the game’s actual flight time before synchronising missiles with a fleet.

sections.title: Run a final check before launch
steps: Confirm the exact target, including planet versus moon, and obtain a recent report of defenses, ABMs and relevant technologies.
Check that the missile action is available from the intended source planet. Confirm range, stock, missile count and primary target.
Estimate the resource cost of intercepted missiles as well as those that reach defenses. Decide whether the resulting fleet operation still has a worthwhile objective.
Coordinate the timing if other strikes are involved, allowing for the defender rebuilding ABMs and for changes since your last report.
Read the final launch details carefully. IPMs cannot be recalled after launch. After impact, inspect the report and update the plan instead of repeating a salvo automatically.

callout.title: A Silo is a tool, not a safety guarantee
callout.text: ABMs do not stop attacking fleets or Moon Destruction missions. Keep your defense plan proportionate and continue fleetsaving; there is no building level that replaces supervision of valuable fleet returns.

checklist: I know which planet benefits from a Nanite upgrade and which queues it can block.
My time estimate uses economy speed and the correct Robotics or Shipyard level.
My intended missile mix fits ABMs + 2 × IPMs ≤ 10 × Silo level.
I checked current ABM stock, range, target type and flight time.
I understand that launching IPMs is irreversible and does not protect my fleet.

guides.title: Build defense around what you need to protect.
guides.summary: Protect routine production, understand the counters, and test the cost of attacking you. Learn how repair, rapid fire, shields and missiles change the result before committing resources to a bunker.
guides.label: Defense doctrine
guides.status: Mechanics reviewed 8 November 2026. Classic formulas are labeled; use current in-game values and your universe settings for exact results.
objectives: Set a defensive budget from your collection interval and realistic local threats.
Choose units for a job instead of copying a universal defense ratio.
Separate combat losses, repaired units and permanent attrition.
Check missile protection, combat bonuses and debris settings before trusting a simulation.

sections.title: Make the routine raid unattractive
paragraphs: Start with a practical goal: protect the production that accumulates between collections, together with vulnerable stationary assets such as satellites and crawlers. Defense is fixed to its location. A stronger bunker does not make a parked fleet or a research savings bank safe, and it cannot replace fleetsaving.

Think like a raider. Their possible return includes loot and recoverable debris; their costs include lost ships, flight fuel and any missile preparation. Your job is to make ordinary attacks unattractive at the amount you actually leave behind. Even then, someone may attack for rivalry, military destruction or amusement. Unprofitability reduces an incentive; it does not grant immunity.

Defense does not slow an incoming fleet's timer. It may make an attacker choose a different fleet or abandon the idea, but once the attack is flying, your response window comes from the mission timing. Keep movable wealth mobile, collect regularly, and preserve fuel for leaving.

example.title: Budget for the collection gap
example.text: Suppose a planet produces 200,000 resources per hour and you normally collect every eight hours. That adds 1.6 million before your next visit. Test defense against that stock plus anything already parked there, not against an empty planet. A 24-hour absence raises the production component to 4.8 million. Changing your collection routine may cost less than buying enough defense for the longer gap. These are illustrative numbers, not a recommended safe stock level.

sections.title: Read the universe before choosing a build
paragraphs: Record the separate ship-debris and defense-debris percentages. Zero defense debris does not mean zero profit: your ships, satellites, crawlers and stored resources can still be the prize. In a defense-into-debris universe, the bunker itself can contribute to the attacker's return. Do not apply the ship percentage to defenses or calculate defense debris from gross battle casualties without checking the simulator's repair treatment.

Also record whether deuterium enters debris, hostile fleet speed, fuel consumption and ACS availability. Faster hostile fleets change your response window. ACS can change the scale of fleet that reaches you. After a merge or settings change, re-run your tests instead of assuming last month's defense target remains useful.

Use opponents that actually exist nearby. A layout tested only against cargo raids tells you little about cruisers, bombers, a mixed fleet or Deathstars. Keep those scenarios separate so you can see which threat the next investment addresses.

sections.title: Give each part of the defense a job
paragraphs: The cheap layer spreads random targeting across more units. Heavy guns supply stronger individual hits. That is a useful planning model, not a physical front line: an attacking shot can randomly hit a Plasma Turret even while thousands of Rocket Launchers remain. A large quantity of weak guns also cannot automatically overcome a shield threshold.

callout.title: A ratio is a test candidate
callout.text: Writing a layout per one Plasma Turret makes comparisons tidy. It does not make that ratio optimal. Price the whole bundle, then test equal-cost alternatives. Do not scrap existing defense just to make the counts match a prettier ratio.

sections.title: Understand rapid fire before adding more fodder
paragraphs: Rapid fire is a chance to take another shot in the same round after hitting an eligible unit type. It is not a damage multiplier or a promise to destroy that many units. For a rapid-fire value r, the repeat chance is 1 − 1/r. At r = 10, the chance is 90%. The extra shot selects a target again; it need not hit the same unit. Destruction of the first target is not required.

The familiar examples are Cruiser versus Rocket Launcher at 10 and Destroyer versus Light Laser at 10. An Ion Cannon has rapid fire 2 against a Reaper. Mixing targets can interrupt a particular attacker's firing chains, but only if the added type is not another favorable target for that attacker. Simply adding one of everything is not an optimization.

Bombers have broad anti-defense rapid fire, including Gauss Cannons and Plasma Turrets in the post-version-7 rules. Plasma avoids Deathstar rapid fire; that does not make it immune to Deathstars or all rapid fire. Read the current in-game rapid-fire panel when testing a matchup. Very old tables predate ship additions and balance changes.

example.title: Change one thing, hold the budget steady
example.text: For a cruiser-heavy test, compare your current cheap layer with an alternative that buys more LL and fewer RL using the same resource valuation. Keep the heavy guns, research and attacker fixed. Then test both layouts against destroyers. The change that helps the first matchup can hurt the second; choose based on your threat mix, not the first favorable result.

sections.title: Shields protect their own unit
paragraphs: Each combat unit has its own shield and hull. A dome is another target with a large shield, not a shared force field that lends shield points to every turret. In the standard combat model, shields regenerate between rounds while hull damage persists through that battle. Surviving units finish the battle repaired; destroyed defenses are handled by the separate reconstruction step.

Small shots can bounce without reducing a strong shield. Compare one shot with the target's effective shield, rather than summing your entire fleet's attack. Older references disagree at the exact 1% boundary, and simulator authors have documented a less-than-or-equal implementation. Avoid planning a valuable fight around equality; check the current simulator and relevant live results.

Weapons, Shielding and Armour Technology change the corresponding stats. The classic technology multiplier is 1 + 0.1 × level. Structural integrity is not the combat hull number: the classic hull starts at structural integrity divided by ten. Modern class and lifeform bonuses must also be included, preferably through a current import.

example.title: Why more weak shots may not help
example.text: A shot worth 40 against an effective shield of 10,000 is only 0.4%. If the attack consists entirely of shots that bounce while that shield remains, adding more identical attackers does not chip it away. A harder-hitting unit may change the battle. This deliberately avoids the disputed exact 1% edge.

sections.title: Count permanent losses after reconstruction
paragraphs: Defenses destroyed in ordinary combat normally reconstruct at about 70%; the Engineer raises the normal recovery figure to about 85%. These are baseline recovery expectations, not guaranteed counts for a small batch or a substitute for checking current modifiers. The Engineer halves the expected permanent share of destroyed defense from 30% to 15% under that model. IPM destruction does not receive this reconstruction.

Losing the battle does not itself erase every defense. Count what was actually destroyed. For each type, remaining = starting − destroyed + repaired. Do not forget reconstruction or add it twice to a result that already includes it. Keep ship wreck-field recovery separate.

Repeated waves still cause attrition. Re-simulate the next wave with the post-repair remainder, not the original bunker. New construction, replenished missiles, changed fleets and different research can all invalidate a simple forecast. A draw can still be costly if the attacker loses nothing and your defenses suffer permanent losses.

example.title: Repeated total destruction: a simplified model
example.text: If every remaining unit were destroyed in each of three separate battles, with no new construction, a constant 70% recovery model leaves 1,000 × 0.7³ = 343. At 85%, it leaves about 614. Real repair rolls and partial destruction vary. The point is that recovery delays erosion; it does not make a bunker permanent.

sections.title: Protect the bunker from missile preparation
paragraphs: IPMs attack defenses independently of a fleet battle. ABMs intercept automatically at one interceptor per incoming missile, consuming both; they do not stop attacking ships. Surviving IPMs bypass shields. The attacker’s Weapons Technology and defender’s Armour Technology matter. Neither a dome nor the Engineer’s ordinary reconstruction bonus provides missile protection.

Missile Silo level 2 unlocks ABMs; level 4 unlocks IPMs with the relevant technology prerequisites. Capacity is ten slots per silo level: an ABM uses one and an IPM uses two. A moon has no missile silo, but its planet's ABMs also defend it. Keep enough capacity and resources to replenish protection rather than assuming one full silo lasts indefinitely.

After interception, the selected primary defense type is attacked. Do not rely on a guaranteed spillover order after it is exhausted. The archived tutorial describes random follow-on targets, while a later developer discussion disputes a fixed order and says the full algorithm was not published. Exact mixed-defense missile predictions deserve verification.

example.title: Count the interception budget first
example.text: A level-5 silo has 50 slots. Forty ABMs plus five IPMs use all 50. If 25 attacking IPMs arrive while those 40 ABMs are still present, the simple interception count is 25 IPMs stopped and 15 ABMs left. A later salvo faces that remainder, not the original inventory. Queued replacements are not available until completed.

sections.title: Use missile formulas as estimates, not launch guarantees
paragraphs: The classic range is 5 × Impulse Drive level − 1 systems within the same galaxy. Impulse 6 therefore gives a 29-system range. The official circular-universe announcement also allows IPM range to wrap when circular solar systems are enabled. Circular galaxies alone do not let a missile cross into another galaxy. Check actual target availability in Galaxy view. Hostile fleet speed affects missile flight time; archived guides disagree on the base expression, so use the current dispatch timing.

A classic damage estimate is surviving IPMs × 12,000 × (1 + 0.1 × attacker Weapons level). Compare that with effective defense hull, not shield points or the displayed structural integrity without conversion. This is an estimate from the older mechanics model: verify applicable modern bonuses and rounding before using it for an exact kill count.

Missiles are spent even when intercepted and cannot be recalled after launch. For a defender, the useful lesson is that armor, stocked ABMs and the ability to replenish all matter; shield upgrades alone do not solve missile exposure. A determined attacker can send repeated salvos or coordinate several launch sites.

example.title: A transparent damage estimate
example.text: Suppose five IPMs survive interception and the attacker has Weapons 10. Ignoring other bonuses, the classic damage budget is 5 × 12,000 × 2 = 120,000. If the selected defense has 20,000 effective hull per unit, that budget corresponds to six units before implementation-specific handling. Keep those assumptions visible; do not turn this teaching example into a promise about a live target.

sections.title: Build in measured stages
steps: Write the job: protect a particular collection interval and specified stationary assets. Set a resource ceiling that leaves room for mines, research, cargo and flight fuel.

Check the technology tree and purchase a small working defense rather than racing to an expensive endgame recipe. Add affordable cheap units and consider domes as they become available. Keep the early economy moving.
Introduce heavier guns when they change the outcome against relevant attacks. Test the next batch against the same threats and stock level used for the baseline.

Compare resource values consistently. If using a hypothetical 3:2:1 trade ratio, metal-equivalent cost is M + 1.5C + 3D. State the ratio and also inspect the real Crystal and Deuterium requirement; equal totals can hide a resource bottleneck.

Compare more units with a combat-research or defense-lifeform upgrade. An upgrade can improve existing defense, but nominal percentages alone do not show whether it crosses a useful survival or damage threshold. Include cost, completion time and the locations actually affected.

Prepare ABMs as defense value and local missile risk grow. After each completed batch, update the saved layout and re-test. Stop expanding when the next spend does not materially improve the protection you need.

callout.title: Avoid the sunk-cost trap
callout.text: After an attack, rebuilding the identical bunker may recreate the identical target. First ask whether less parked wealth, a different collection interval, a safer fleet routine or a targeted composition change solves the problem more cheaply.

example.title: A first defense session
example.text: On one young production planet, record the next collection time and expected stock. Inspect affordable RL/LL batches and the Small Shield Dome prerequisite in the technology tree. Compare a small cargo-only raid before and after the proposed purchase. Add a light combat escort to the attacker and test again. Build only the affordable batch that addresses your current exposure, then return to your economic goal. Repeat later with heavier threats rather than scaling the first recipe forever.

sections.title: Make the simulator answer the real question
paragraphs: Use a simulator maintained for the current game version, with the in-game simulator as a useful starting point. A tool being listed in an old guide is not evidence that it still works. Large-battle calculations and simulator inputs have received fixes, including live version 12.5.4 in January 2026. A PTS announcement alone does not establish behavior on your live server.

Import a recent report where possible, then inspect what arrived. Missing research or bonuses must be treated as unknown, not as zero. For a costly decision, compare several runs and plausible unfavorable inputs. Record variation in losses and draws, not just the prettiest average. A narrow simulated margin is a reason for caution.
steps: Check every attacking and defending fleet, all defense counts and both domes. Include satellites, crawlers and ships that will actually be present at impact.
Verify Weapons, Shielding and Armour levels, player class, relevant lifeform bonuses and Engineer status. Avoid manually adding a bonus that the import already includes.
Check ship and defense debris percentages, deuterium-in-debris, fuel settings, coordinates and loot assumptions. The resources present at impact may exceed those on the earlier spy report.
Compare attacker win/draw/loss, attacker ship losses and fuel, debris they could recover, your permanent losses after reconstruction and the cost to restore production assets.
Run cargo raids, local fast fleets, bomber-heavy attacks and Deathstar scenarios separately. For follow-up waves, carry the post-repair result forward and account for missile preparation first.
Save the assumptions and compare them with real reports when available. Investigate a mismatch before committing to another large build based on the same model.

sections.title: When an attack is already coming
paragraphs: Confirm the destination, arrival time and what is actually exposed. Move ships and resources through a suitable fleetsave while you still can; do not wait for a new defensive batch to rescue a clearly losing position. Verify that any construction you are counting on finishes before impact.

Check the missile inventory after a salvo, not just the old espionage or build screen. Ask alliance members for help only with enough time and accurate details to coordinate. A defending fleet can change both combat and debris profitability, so it belongs in the simulation rather than being treated as free protection.

Afterward, read the report and inspect the location. Record actual repaired defense, surviving production assets, missing cargo capacity and replacement costs. Repair the operational problem first. The goal is to resume a sustainable routine without leaving the same profitable opportunity behind again.

checklist: I know the stock and stationary assets my defense is intended to protect.
I checked separate ship and defense debris settings, hostile speed and ACS.
I tested realistic attackers with current research, lifeform bonuses and complete unit counts.
I understand that domes have their own shields and rapid fire is probabilistic.
I used post-repair losses and remaining counts when assessing follow-up waves.
I checked ABM inventory and shared silo capacity, including protection for the moon.
I have a fleetsave and collection routine instead of relying on a bunker for parked wealth.

objectives: Prioritize economic upgrades without ignoring energy, cargo or fleet safety.
Use a Rock’tal-oriented building plan as a candidate, not an automatic empire-wide switch.
Compare mine, crawler, energy and lifeform investments on the same net-income basis.

sections.title: Choose the routine before the bonuses
sections.body: This path fits an account whose income should keep arriving when the player cannot repeatedly launch expeditions or hunt targets. Collector is the natural class to compare for production and crawler support, but choose it against your current bonuses and real activity. A class switch has a cost and can alter logistics. A few excellent expedition days do not prove that a permanently active schedule will suit you.

callout.title: Passive income still needs collection
callout.text: Mines do not need relaunching, but storage fills, ships return and resources become targets. The miner routine is less click-intensive, not unattended.

sections.title: Stage 1: make every existing planet productive
steps: Audit each planet’s next mine level, available energy, storage window and collection route. Fix a production shortage before buying more capacity that cannot run.
Compare the next useful mine upgrades across planets. Include supporting energy and the resource that limits your current account goal.
Maintain cargo and flight fuel for regular collection. Leave enough capacity to protect your stock between visits.
Expand a weak colony in manageable batches. Do not spend all available resources bringing every planet to the same arbitrary level if a smaller plan has better return.
sections.body: Use the economy guide’s incremental payback method. Resource weights must be consistent across cost and extra net production. If you value Deuterium differently because of trading or a fuel goal, state that assumption instead of hiding it inside the result.

sections.title: Stage 2: solve the power and crawler system together
paragraphs: Crawlers connect production directly to power demand. Before filling the active crawler limit, check the next batch’s actual energy requirement and net mine gain. If you need additional fusion, include the reactor cost and operating Deuterium. If you need satellites, account for their vulnerability and your ability to rebuild power after a raid.

Read the fusion table before deciding that more Solar Plant levels are always the cheapest option. Higher Energy Technology improves fusion output across the account. At a fixed energy demand it may allow lower reactor utilization and less fuel consumption. Research is an empire-wide purchase; compare its effect across every reactor that will benefit, not just the planet you happen to be viewing.

After any crawler or energy change, compare final total production and net Deuterium with the old setup. The attractive number is the additional income you keep after supplying the power, not only the displayed percentage boost.

sections.title: Stage 3: develop a production lifeform plan
paragraphs: Rock’tal is a candidate for its mining-focused buildings. Start with one planet, identify the next useful population slot and price the housing, food, tier infrastructure and technology together. Reaching a distant slot is not automatically better than improving an affordable technology you already have.

Choose production, energy or cost-saving technologies for the job you need. The selected species determines local buildings; available Lifeform technologies are not restricted to that species after discovery. Use the Lifeforms guide to compare named options and keep Intergalactic Envoys active where needed for continued discovery.

Spread early, economical research levels where they are affordable rather than chasing one very high local level without comparison. Compare the cost of unlocking another planet’s slot against the gain from a higher level on an established planet. A reset or species switch can interrupt the current setup, so plan it deliberately instead of converting every planet at once.

sections.title: Run one investment queue, not four competing ones

example.title: Illustrative priority decision
example.text: A mine project costs 12 million planning units and adds 300,000 net per day: 40 days. A crawler-plus-power project costs 9 million and adds 300,000: 30 days. The crawler project wins this simple comparison, unless it consumes fuel or Crystal reserved for a more important near-term unlock. Include the same resource weights and supporting costs on both sides.

sections.body: Keep a short queue: one funded improvement, one next target and one optional alternative. Recheck after class changes, new colonies or an expiring bonus. Keep a reserve for transport, energy recovery and fleet safety. A miner with a fragile logistics chain can lose more in one neglected return than a carefully chosen upgrade earns in weeks.

checklist: My storage and collection plan fit my actual offline interval.
Crawler comparisons include power and net Deuterium costs.
I evaluated Energy Technology across the reactors that benefit.
My next Lifeform purchase has a specific output benefit and full unlock cost.

guides.title: The expedition path: build an operation you can repeat.
guides.summary: A development order for players who launch regularly: enough cargo, enough fuel, sensible lifeform choices and a routine that survives bad luck.
guides.label: Play-style strategy
guides.status: Conditional Skie strategy based on the October 2026 administrator expedition guide; class and patch modifiers must match your universe
objectives: Build a reliable expedition cycle before investing in its maximum theoretical output.
Choose Lifeform upgrades by the bottleneck they remove.
Track spendable resources, ship finds, fuel and losses separately.

sections.title: Count the launches you will really make
sections.body: This path rewards regular attention. Discoverer is the class to compare first for an expedition-centered account, but use the current class bonuses and your universe’s actual rules. Start with the hours you can relaunch, not the hours a spreadsheet assumes you are awake. Record a normal week including workdays and weekends. Mines remain valuable income while you cannot launch.

callout.title: Do not fund the plan with a lucky screenshot
callout.text: Resources and useful ship finds vary. Black holes, hostile encounters, empty results and delays are part of the operation. Keep a replacement reserve before expanding it.

sections.title: Stage 1: build the working fleet and schedule
steps: Read the expedition mechanics guide. Confirm Astrophysics, total fleet slots, class, economy speed, relevant bonuses and the current reward bracket before calculating a fleet.
Create one replaceable expedition fleet with sufficient cargo and the appropriate support ships. Keep your core transport and fleetsave capacity separate.
Run a test cycle. Inspect the report and actual returning cargo. Check whether your normal launch time leads to a return you can cover.
Repeat only across the slots you can maintain. Save the last batch’s landing window with extra margin for delays before your planned offline time.
sections.body: An expedition build has two different limits: the reward the mechanics allow and the cargo you can bring home. More cargo can solve a transport limit, but excess cargo does not endlessly raise the reward cap. Likewise, travel-speed improvements help only when shorter travel becomes an extra real cycle or a more reliable schedule.

sections.title: Stage 2: grow the bottleneck, not everything at once
paragraphs: If reports show insufficient carrying capacity, correct cargo before buying another reward bonus. If fleets sit at home after returning, a speed upgrade may do little for daily launches. If you cannot replace a lost working fleet, build the reserve before increasing launch size. If fuel interrupts the routine, fix Deuterium logistics rather than measuring success only in gross loot.

Once the operation is stable, compare slot-unlocking research, cargo capacity and reward bonuses. Price the entire change, including any extra fleet required for a new slot. Astrophysics that adds capacity is not free income if you cannot afford or relaunch the new fleet.

Keep a daily record of launches, resource returns, usable ship finds, fuel and losses. Treat findable ships separately from resources until you have a real use or conversion plan. A resource-weighting method must match your objective; a large Metal-equivalent total can still leave you short of Crystal for research.

sections.title: Stage 3: choose Lifeforms around the operation
paragraphs: Compare the building benefits of Humans, Mecha and Rock’tal against your actual split of expedition and mining income. Do not confuse a planet’s chosen species with the technologies selected into its research slots. Once species are discovered, you can assemble research choices across species while keeping the buildings that fit that planet.

Review Enhanced Sensor Technology, Sixth Sense and Telekinetic Tractor Beam for expedition-focused technology choices. Discoverer Enhancement is relevant when you are actually playing Discoverer. Use the current descriptions and compare the next level’s benefit with the cost to unlock and develop it. The Lifeforms guide explains the population and artefact work needed first.

Cargo or speed selections can be sensible logistics choices, but they displace another technology in the same slot. Estimate the production you give up and ask whether the change increases useful capacity, actual cycles or quality of life. A percentage-point change in an additive bonus is not the same percentage change in your final account income.

sections.title: Rebalance when your routine changes

example.title: A useful cargo decision
example.text: If a fleet can already carry its permitted maximum find, another cargo upgrade may reduce the number of cargo ships required per launch. That can lower replacement exposure or simplify logistics. It does not by itself prove higher rewards. Measure the benefit you are actually buying.

sections.body: Review several days or a meaningful batch, not one exceptional result. Change one variable at a time. If work or life reduces your launches, shift investment toward passive production rather than maintaining an old high-attention plan out of habit. The best expedition account is one that you can keep operating without sacrificing fleet safety or sleep.

checklist: My fleet calculation uses the current account and universe inputs.
I retain transport capacity, fuel and a replacement reserve outside expedition fleets.
My next cargo, speed or LF upgrade solves a real measured limit.
I record net returns across a batch and separate ships from spendable resources.

guides.title: The active-fleet path: logistics before firepower.
guides.summary: Develop ships around a specific mission, simulate the risk, and keep the fleet safe enough to fly again tomorrow.
guides.label: Play-style strategy
guides.status: Conditional strategy and risk-management workflow, not a universal combat composition or current combat formula
objectives: Define the task a combat fleet must perform before buying ships.
Account for fuel, cargo, recovery and an exit plan in a raid decision.
Select class and Lifeform support for the ships and missions you really use.

sections.title: Decide what your fleet is for
paragraphs: An active fleet is an operating expense as well as an asset. Decide whether you want small profitable raids, organized alliance combat, debris collection or another specific activity. Those goals require different speed, cargo and fighting capability. General is the class to compare for combat-focused activity, but class bonuses do not turn an unsuitable fleet into a profitable one.

Begin with a role you can evaluate and a fleet you can afford to replace. Do not copy a fixed battleship-to-fighter ratio from an unrelated account. Enemy composition, technologies, defenses, universe settings and allied participation can change the result. A combat simulator is part of planning, not a license to assume a win.

sections.title: Stage 1: make the support system reliable
steps: Learn fleetsaving and practise the route with a small fleet. Know where the main fleet will go when you are offline and how you will cover the return.
Prepare enough Deuterium for the intended flight and the next safe move. A successful attack can still strand a fleet if you spend its last fuel.
Provide cargo for the intended resource recovery and appropriate recycling capacity when debris collection is part of the plan. Do not count a debris field as recovered profit before it is collected.
Use research and facilities to unlock the ships and handling capacity required for the chosen role. Do not fund extra combat hulls while basic fuel and transport are missing.

callout.title: Defenses cannot protect an unattended valuable fleet
callout.text: They can change an attacker’s calculation, but a sufficiently valuable target can justify a larger attack. The fleet’s movement and landing plan remain essential.

sections.title: Stage 2: use a launch decision checklist
paragraphs: Read the most relevant intelligence you can obtain. Check what the report actually reveals and what remains unknown. Simulate with the technologies, ships, defenses and universe settings you can support. If a missing input could change the result, run a conservative case or do not take the fight. The simulation is only as reliable as the information entered.

Calculate expected usable loot and collectable debris, then subtract fuel and expected replacement losses in a consistent resource valuation. Allow for the possibility that the target moves, reinforcements arrive or someone else collects debris. Your original expected outcome is not guaranteed because the fleet has launched.
steps: Confirm the intended target, mission type, chosen fleet, speed and arrival time.
Check that you can monitor the relevant flight and landing window and have a safe post-return plan.
Review current rules governing attacks and allied coordination in your universe. Do not infer permission from another server’s settings.
After dispatch, verify the event list and continue monitoring for material changes. If the situation no longer matches the plan, reassess rather than treating the original simulation as binding.

sections.title: Stage 3: support the fleet you actually fly
paragraphs: Read the Lifeform technologies that apply to your chosen ship classes, fuel, speed, cargo or combat characteristics. Compare their benefit with normal combat or engine research and with simply buying the missing support ships. A technology for a ship you rarely use can be poor value despite an impressive percentage.

Mecha is a candidate to examine for fleet-oriented buildings, not a compulsory identity. Planet species, selected research and account class are separate layers. You can preserve an economic building setup while selecting a useful technology from another discovered species. Pilot changes on one suitable planet and record the actual bonus before repeating them across the account.
Research that changes speed can change your usual return schedule. Recheck travel times and fleetsave plans after upgrades. A stronger fleet with a return you cannot cover is not a safer fleet.

sections.title: Review the operation, including the miss

example.title: A failed raid is still data
example.text: If the target moved and the fleet returned empty, record fuel spent, the observation you missed and whether the flight left other commitments exposed. Do not erase the result from the average. A routine with frequent empty flights can be less profitable than a smaller, better-qualified set of targets.

sections.body: Keep reports and lessons in an appropriate private place. Public guides do not need real coordinates, fleet schedules, names or account screenshots. Review the sequence: intelligence, decision, launch, monitoring, collection and safe return. Improve the weakest step before increasing the fleet’s value. Alliance cooperation details will live in their own section once its mechanics and operating procedures are confirmed.

checklist: My fleet has a named role and a funded fuel/transport/recovery plan.
I understand the limits of the intelligence and simulation behind the decision.
My fleet return is covered by a current fleetsaving and attendance plan.
Lifeform and research choices support the ships I actually use.

guides.title: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
guides.summary: What to build first when Orion is enabled, how to spread IAS levels across planets, and a clearly bounded estimate of how total IAS might translate into rewards.
guides.label: Merge preparation
guides.status: Orion preparation reviewed 9 November 2026. Confirm activation and prices in your destination universe. Historical cost projections and hypothetical rewards are labelled separately.
objectives: Follow a practical first-build sequence once Orion is active in your destination.
Separate total IAS progression, Lithium throughput, mission completion and reward claims.
Use a worked IAS-to-reward scenario without mistaking it for a verified reward formula.

sections.title: At the merge, confirm the feature before spending
paragraphs: Plan for Orion as part of the move, then check the destination itself. The US merge announcement lists Mars and Nembus as target universes and gives a 9–12 November 2026 merge window. It does not explicitly confirm their Orion activation flag. Both are newly created merge targets; that alone does not prove that the feature is on or off.

The official version 13.1.0 notice limits its 6 November Orion activation to universes launching that day. Gameforge’s launch release says a global rollout is planned for 30 November. Neither statement settles the merge targets individually. Open the destination’s technology tree and check that the IAS, Lithium conversion and anomaly interface are available before committing a build budget.

callout.title: Use this guide when Orion is enabled
callout.text: The sequence below is a conditional merge-day plan, not a claim that a named target is already active. The live technology tree supplies the exact prerequisites, fields, construction prices and restrictions. A missing feature is a reason to wait, not to rebuild around an assumed release date.

sections.title: What to build first, and why
sections.body: Keep your mines, energy and fleet-safety routine working. Orion adds another use for resources and attention; it does not replace the economy that pays for it. This is a spending order, not a fixed timetable or a requirement to use Dark Matter.
steps: Check the live prerequisites and spare fields on each planet you can practically supply. Build the minimum prerequisite facilities needed to place an IAS there. Do not add expensive facilities solely because an old PTS screenshot had them.

Place IAS level 1 buildings across those usable planets. For a target total, buy the cheapest next scanner level available, rather than pushing one planet far ahead. Equal per-planet exponential prices make a balanced network the least-resource route to that total.

Aim first for a modest total such as IAS 50, then stop to run the loop. Enable a small, affordable Lithium conversion workload and read both the hourly input and output. Check the current storage limit; leave a reserve for claiming the reward as well as finding the mission.

Scan for a manageable mission, inspect its actual level, type, stars, waves, participation rules, duration, requirements and reward claim cost. Use ships or delivery cargo you can afford to commit, and cover the return. A large possible reward is not a completed or claimed reward. Check the claim deadline and actual reward-delivery destination; do not assume the reward can wait until your next login.

Complete the qualifying mission and confirm the Control Center unlock. Buy a low level of a relevant bonus building only after its effect and price make sense for the missions you actually run. A ship-focused building has little immediate value if you keep choosing resource rewards.

Advance through the next useful checkpoints: 100, 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 total IAS. Recheck affordable missions, Lithium supply and claim costs at each step. Continue beyond a checkpoint only when it supports a mission or bonus you can use.

Buy extra discovery capacity, scan results or deeper bonus-building levels only when the existing limit is regularly stopping profitable play. More slots are not more income if you cannot fund claims or finish missions.

callout.title: Balanced levels optimize access, not everything
callout.text: The cheapest network for a given total IAS is not automatically the best Lithium-throughput layout. Local scanner levels, conversion workload, input availability and current bonuses also matter. First solve the access target; then measure the bottleneck before specializing a planet.

sections.title: Total IAS is the sum across your planets
paragraphs: Use T = L1 + L2 + … + Ln, where each L is one eligible planet’s IAS level. Total IAS supports the selectable anomaly level. It is not the exact level of every result, a reward multiplier by itself, or a building level on one planet. Read the mission card and the live unlock requirement.

For a balanced plan from level zero across n planets, set q = floor(T / n) and r = T − n × q. Build r planets to q + 1 and the other n − r to q. Existing uneven accounts should compare the next available upgrade prices instead of demolishing anything to match an illustration.

The table uses 15 hypothetical, equally priced and usable planets. It is not an account requirement. Amounts are cumulative construction costs from IAS 0, in units of each named resource, calculated with the preserved beta13 cost model. They are not current live quotes and do not include prerequisites.

example.title: Why distribute the levels?
example.text: In the same historical model, total IAS 350 across 15 planets costs 32,992,180 Metal. Across 10 planets at level 35 each, it costs 2,446,262,300 Metal. The total access level is the same; the second plan buys much deeper, more expensive local levels. This comparison isolates construction cost. It does not say the two layouts have equal Lithium output or equal real-world setup costs.

sections.title: Build toward a useful unlock, then complete the mission
sections.body: The public beta13 field research recorded the progression below. Use these as planning checkpoints to confirm in the current Control Center, not guaranteed present-day bonus coefficients. Reaching the total IAS alone did not unlock the building: completing the qualifying mission was the trigger. The actual discovered mission level can differ from the level selected for a scan.

rows: Ship rewards, if those are part of your routine.
Lithium-related rewards; verify its current effect after beta16.
Lower resource input for Lithium conversion in the historical tests.

callout.title: 350 is a progression milestone, not a universal first purchase
callout.text: The historical guide used 350 to reach the final recorded building unlock. That does not prove rushing there has the best payback. A smaller account can stop earlier while it learns mission costs; an established account can advance faster if it can fund and complete the missions. In particular, recheck the Lithium Electrolysis Lab and Anomaly Analysis Center effects in current Techinfo rather than treating this old table as a current bonus specification.

sections.title: A basic IAS-to-reward extrapolation, with its limits
paragraphs: The official FAQ says higher anomaly levels bring better potential rewards alongside higher difficulty and costs. It does not publish a function that converts total IAS into a precise reward. Mission type, actual level, stars, wave count, PvE or PvP mode, class and bonuses, participation and partial claims can all change the result. Historical samples differ in several of these at once, so fitting one curve through them would be misleading.

For a simple planning sensitivity test, suppose selectable mission level tracks total IAS T and the gross Metal reward per fully completed and fully claimed mission rises linearly with T. This linear relationship is unverified. Also suppose an illustrative baseline R0 = 1,000,000 Metal per mission at T0 = 100, and N = 2 such missions completed and claimed per day. These are invented inputs for arithmetic, not observed rewards or a daily mission limit.

The assumed formulas are R(T) = R0 × T / T0 Metal per mission and Gday(T) = N × R(T) Metal per day. Hold mission template, stars, number of waves, mode, class, bonuses and participation constant; assume the whole reward is claimed. The table is gross reward before any cost, failure or loss. It excludes ships, items, Dark Matter and chance Lithium, which cannot be added directly to Metal.

example.title: What the scenario tells you
example.text: Under this assumption only, moving from total IAS 100 to 350 makes the same completed mission worth 3.5 times as much. If Lithium costs or time let you finish only one mission per day at 350 instead of two at 100, the illustrated daily total is 3.5 million versus 2 million Metal, only 1.75 times as much. Neither ratio predicts the live game.

callout.title: This is not a verified reward formula or income forecast
callout.text: Do not spend on the promise of these numbers. There is no measured error range, guaranteed minimum or demonstrated linear scaling here. Real rewards can be lower, absent, or outweighed by costs and losses. Replace the baseline and test the relationship with comparable current mission reports before using it for a budget.

sections.title: Replace the scenario with your own measured return
steps: Record the game version, total IAS and actual mission level separately. Keep the mission type, stars, mode, waves, class, bonuses, participation and claim fraction alongside each result. Compare like with like.
Record the total actually claimed across the mission, not one wave copied as a whole-mission total or the possible reward shown before completion. Treat an unknown value as unknown.

For a given IAS band, divide the total actual reward by all attempted comparable missions if you want a return that includes failed attempts. Keep reward per successful full claim as a separate measure. Several observations are more informative than one lucky card.

Observe a full real day or week, including waiting for Lithium, travel and attention. The simplest gross daily return is total actually claimed over that period divided by elapsed days. Keep denominators matched: average per attempt × attempts per day, or average per successful full claim × successful full claims per day. Never multiply an average that already includes failures by successful completions only.

Subtract the resources spent producing the Lithium for scans and claims, plus delivery costs, fuel and unrecovered fleet losses. Use a stated exchange rate if combining Metal, Crystal and Deuterium into one value. Do not treat Lithium as free because it is produced in a building.

Compare the measured extra daily net return with the price of the next IAS upgrades. A rough payback is upgrade cost divided by extra daily net return, in the same value units. If the extra return is zero or negative, that calculation gives no positive payback.

example.title: More IAS can lose to better throughput
example.text: Suppose two otherwise comparable routines return 2 million Metal per day and 3.5 million Metal per day before costs. If their daily input, fuel and loss costs are 0.5 million and 2.5 million Metal-equivalent respectively, net return is 1.5 million versus 1 million. These are hypothetical arithmetic inputs. A larger gross reward is not enough to justify an upgrade.

sections.title: Patch changes that an old Orion guide can miss
sections.body: The preserved source is guide 0.19.6, dated 11 October 2026, commit 56a951b, describing PTS v13.1.0 beta13. Later official changes take precedence. This list explains specific limits; it is not a complete changelog or a claim that beta17 is the newest release.

rows: IAS construction scaling changed from 1.4 to 1.5; Lithium base production changed to 15.36.
Old cost and production estimates must be version-labelled.
Discard the old unlimited-storage claim; check the current cap.
Explicit Lithium rewards removed; any reward claim can give additional Lithium by chance.
Do not budget guaranteed Lithium from a mission reward.
Earlier ship-yield samples cannot quote present-day returns.

callout.title: No universal Lithium-income calculator
callout.text: The old production example used an inferred ×10 economy factor and lacked fresh post-rebalance validation. It is not used here as a current income prediction. Read live hourly input/output and storage figures instead.

sections.title: What the preserved cost model calculates
paragraphs: For the historical IAS model, the base resource costs are 84 Metal, 42 Crystal and 14 Deuterium. At target level L, the formula is floor(Base × 1.5^(L − 1)) separately for each resource. A current-to-target result sums each next level through the target. The implementation uses exact integer arithmetic with 3/2, not floating-point estimates.

The beta13 official notes increased the scaling factor from 1.4 to 1.5. The preserved calculator follows 1.5, represented exactly as 3/2. Its outputs remain historical projections and require a live-price check before use.

This calculator prices one planet only. A combined account target of 350 means adding the scanner levels on all eligible planets; do not type 350 into a single-planet target field. For a network, calculate each planet separately and add the same resource columns. Prices exclude prerequisites, facilities, transport and opportunity cost.

example.title: Worked historical example: IAS 0 → 2
example.text:
Level 1: 84 Metal + 42 Crystal + 14 Deuterium.
Level 2: 126 Metal + 63 Crystal + 21 Deuterium.
Combined projection: 210 Metal + 105 Crystal + 35 Deuterium.
This verifies the calculation method, not today’s in-game pricing.

sections.title: A final check before the next build
steps: Confirm Orion activation, current prerequisites, construction prices and your usable planets in the destination universe.
Keep total IAS, each local IAS level, actual mission level and completed-mission unlocks separate.
Compare one live construction price against the historical model before using its network table or calculator. A mismatch means stop relying on that projection.
Reserve enough Lithium for the scan and the reward claim, and price the ordinary resources used to make it.
Use actual claimed rewards and sustainable completion rates to decide on the next checkpoint. Keep private coordinates, planet names, balances, fleet details and screenshots out of public research.

checklist: Orion is enabled in my destination, and I have checked its current prices and prerequisites.
I have a balanced access target, a Lithium budget and a manageable first mission.
I know that a qualifying completed mission, not total IAS alone, triggers a recorded building unlock.
I am treating the reward table as a hypothetical scenario, not a verified formula or promised daily income.
My next upgrade is justified by current costs and actual returns, not only a possible reward card.
